extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator; literate London coffee-house public (early-18th-century urban readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and moral guidance for composing periodical essays, satire, news items, and devotional verse for the Spectator-style readership. Covers what counts as good/bad wit, the ethics of anonymous and defamatory publication, and what makes news valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalness in writing ('Natural' is pleasing and easie)
rubrics_metrics.description: That which the Wits call Natural is 'that which is pleasing and easie.' Natural writing should present new thought without affected ornament; smooth quaint language and forced conceits are mere frothy amusements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid over-polished, speculative 'fine things' and ornament for its own sake. Beware the 'new Thought or Conceit dressed up in smooth quaint Language' — these are labelled 'meer frothy Amusements! fit only for Boys or silly Women to be caught with.' Aim for plainness, usefulness, and sound observation rather than speculative affectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity in publication (benefit to learning and trial)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposal to force every author to swear his name and register would 'have effectually suppressed all printed Scandal,' but would also 'destroy Learning' — many celebrated works first appear anonymously as a trial before the author owns them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize anonymous publication as an important stage for new writers and for the emergence of works of genius. Requiring upfront disclosure of authorship is an anti-pattern: it would 'operate promiscuously, and root up the Corn and Tares together.' Treat anonymity as a legitimate condition for initial circulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defamatory libels are scandalous and morally blameworthy
rubrics_metrics.description: Defamatory Papers and Pamphlets are 'so scandalous to a Government, and detestable in the Eyes of all good Men'; scurrility and billingsgate pass for wit, and attacks—even when 'supported with the appearances of Truth'—are marks of an evil mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not make personal defamation the instrument of satire. Calling-names, ribaldry, lampooning private honour, and 'tearing to Pieces the Reputation' of competitors are condemned as destructive to public truth and humane society. Satire that relies on scurrility is an anti-pattern that cheapens virtue and reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readers/dispersers of libel share moral culpability
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who take Pleasure in reading and dispersing defamatory Libels are 'as guilty as if they had composed them' — approval of libel equates to advising or sanctioning the crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and publishers should understand that circulation and approbation of libel are morally (and historically legally) culpable acts. Examples/authorities: Bayle; St. Gregory's practice of holding readers responsible; Roman law punishing approvers and dispersers as authors. Anti-pattern: passive consumption and sharing of defamatory pieces without protest.

rubrics_metrics.name: State enforcement/punishment as deterrent to libel
rubrics_metrics.description: If a Government would inflict exemplary Punishment on an Author who supports a cause with Falsehood and Scandal, 'we should quickly see an End put to this Race of Vermin.' Historically, libel was severely punished (Roman law, death in some instances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an expressly proposed policy-standard: exemplary public punishment of defamatory writers would deter libel. Practical implication for editors/policymakers: public penalties (or palpable consequences) are effective at curbing rampant slander, though the essay warns about overbroad measures that may chill learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness = novelty and matters of fact ('all matters of fact which a man did not know before are News')
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers delight in anything that is new to them; 'A Victory, or a Defeat, are equally agreeable... they have a Relish for every thing that is News, let the matter of it be what it will.' Novelty and newly learned facts drive the appetite for news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing news items or reports, prioritize information that is genuinely new to the readership. Novel particulars satisfy curiosity; repetition of known facts is less valuable. Anti-pattern: filling pages with rehashes of what the public already knows without new particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer local, immediate, and useful intelligence to repeated distant dispatches
rubrics_metrics.description: The essay recommends applying curiosity to History, Travels, or local occurrences: a proposed daily paper covering events within ten miles would give readers 'News fresh and fresh' and be more useful than repeated dispatches from Zug, Bender, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For periodical/newspaper producers: consider focusing on proximate, verifiable local intelligence (cheap carriage, daily receipt) and sustained genres (history/travel) that give perpetual fuel for curiosity. Example specimen items (horse in the pound, dozen weddings, stray animals) illustrate that local detail can satisfy readers' appetite. Anti-pattern: privileging distant war dispatches that merely sustain an endless thirst without lasting value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid redundant repetition and excessive commentary on the same tale
rubrics_metrics.description: Although several papers may receive the same intelligence 'very often in the same Words,' their 'Way of Cooking it is so different' — but the multiplication of the same text and annotations wastes readers' time and creates an unsatisfying repetition of the same tale across multiple venues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and writers should avoid needless duplication of identical reports across many papers and refrain from manufacturing variations that add little substance. Instead supply fresh particulars, synthesis, or genuinely new remarks. Anti-pattern: serial reprinting and superfluous commentary that keeps the public in 'a perpetual Gape after Knowledge' without real improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Christian/divine poetry should employ gratitude and exalt the Maker
rubrics_metrics.description: Christian poets possess a superior subject — the Supreme Being — which 'fills with every thing that can raise the Imagination.' The Spectator recommends Christian poets publish divine hymns and odes celebrating God's providence and mercies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing devotional verse, aim for heartfelt gratitude, sublime subject-matter, and sustained praise that elevates the soul; such works can surpass pagan examples. Practical note: the editor will publish suitable divine poetry (the Spectator includes an example hymn), indicating editorial encouragement of this subgenre.
